extractions.description: A theoretical and critical analysis of AI scaling-law claims, especially how evaluation metrics, population sampling, subgroup heterogeneity, and value pluralism complicate claims that model performance universally improves with larger datasets, models, or compute. The paper synthesizes prior machine-learning and social-science literature and reports no new computational experiments.

type.quote: We draw on empirical results from machine learning and scholarship from the social sciences to interrogate the validity of claims made about scaling laws
type.justification: The paper develops a conceptual argument from prior literature rather than reporting newly executed experiments.

name.quote: We ground our analysis in the development of scaling laws for AI
name.justification: The paper directly critiques and develops implications for research on AI scaling laws.

name.quote: Evaluation of AI systems involves computing and comparing quantitative measures of performance of a system on a task.
name.justification: A central contribution concerns the validity and social contingency of AI evaluation metrics.

name.quote: We draw on and extend recent work in the responsible AI and computational social science communities
name.justification: The argument extends responsible-AI scholarship concerning metrics, fairness, values, and affected communities.

name.quote: We draw on and extend recent work in the responsible AI and computational social science communities
name.justification: Computational social science provides concepts and evidence used to analyze populations, sampling, representation, and metrics.

name.quote: In the context of multilingual language modeling, the curse of multilinguality refers to the degradation of model performance across languages
name.justification: Multilingual language modeling is used as an important motivating setting, but the paper does not contribute a new multilingual model or experiment.

name.quote: Such approaches have been the foundation of high-profile evaluations of machine learning failures
name.justification: The paper advances claims about subgroup disparities, incompatible metrics, and fairness in model evaluation.

name.quote: including natural language processing (e.g., BLEU (Reiter 2018; Post 2018), ROUGE (Ganesan 2018))
name.justification: Natural language processing supplies examples and cited evaluation practices, but the paper does not introduce an NLP system.

name.quote: although initial results demonstrated scaling laws for natural language processing tasks, similar laws have been developed for multimodal and reinforcement learning models
name.justification: Multimodal learning and reinforcement learning are discussed as application settings for scaling laws rather than experimentally advanced.

name.quote: although initial results demonstrated scaling laws for natural language processing tasks, similar laws have been developed for multimodal and reinforcement learning models
name.justification: Reinforcement learning is cited as another setting in which scaling laws have been studied.

name.quote: Methods have been developed from participatory democracy (Polletta 2012), deliberation theory (Fishkin and Luskin 2005), and value-sensitive design
name.justification: The paper recommends participatory and community-based approaches as part of future AI research practice.
